title: Swiss-roll DRAM: self-rolling nanomembrane turns one planar array into 50 tiers
idea: Scale jump from meter-scale battery jelly-rolls down to microns: fabricate a planar oxide-semiconductor 1T1C array on a pre-strained SiNx/SiNx bilayer, undercut it, and let the strain roll it into a ~10-um tube of ~50 windings; radial vias are electroplated afterwards through windows that line up after rolling. One lithography pass yields ~50 stacked tiers.
why: Attacks 3D's need for 26+ tiers and the litho cost of each tier (facts 2, 4): tier count comes from mechanics rather than deposition and etch loops, claiming ~20-50x bits per litho layer.

title: Vertical bucket brigade: charge hops tier-to-tier down to one sense tier
idea: Take the astronomy CCD and rotate its shift axis to vertical: stacked storage tiers linked by gated vertical channels clock charge packets down plane by plane to a single bottom tier of sense amps, so 64 storage tiers need no periphery of their own. Time split: dense tiers hold charge for ms, and a whole-plane shift takes ns per hop.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7), and per-tier wordline and sense wiring blocks 3D (fact 2); one sense tier for 64 storage tiers could cut periphery area per bit by >10x.

title: Hot-aisle/cold-aisle tier zoning with embedded heat-spreader planes
idea: Scale datacenter airflow zoning down to a 3D die: insert a 50-nm AlN or diamond-like-carbon heat-spreader plane every 16 tiers, tie the planes to sidewall thermal vias, and put logic-heavy tiers at the hot end and cell tiers at the cold end. Leakage halves for every ~10 C, so a 20 C cooler cell tier needs a quarter of the refresh.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) and the thermal wall of tall stacks: ~4x less refresh, and more tiers can sit over hot logic.

title: Tier-wide back-gate plane flips cells between sprint and hibernate modes
idea: Time-multiplex the transistor threshold: each thin-film tier sits on its own buried back-gate plate, biased toward low Vt during active windows (ns to us) and swung negative during idle (seconds) to raise Vt by ~0.4 V, which cuts subthreshold leakage by ~10^4 and stretches refresh from 64 ms to seconds. It needs one plate per tier and no wiring per cell.
why: The leakage tail forces refresh (fact 3); fast access and long retention from the same cell target >10x lower refresh energy.

title: Undiced wafer-scale DRAM face-bonded to a wafer-scale accelerator
idea: Jump from die to wafer: keep the 300-mm DRAM wafer whole, use programmable links stitched at each reticle boundary to route around dead mats, and hybrid-bond it face-to-face to a wafer-scale compute wafer so each compute tile gets a multi-GB slab directly above it. No dicing kerf, packages, TSVs or PHYs.
why: Removes the HBM TSV and package tax (fact 6) and data-movement energy (fact 5): ~0.1 pJ/bit vertical access versus 3-4 pJ/bit for HBM.

title: Skyscraper sky-lobbies: express vertical lines to zone decoders every 16 tiers
idea: Copy high-rise elevator design: split a 256-tier stack into 16-tier zones, run a few express vertical lines to a lobby tier in each zone that holds thin-film local decoders, and limit each zone's staircase to 16 steps. Contact area then grows with the log of tier count instead of linearly.
why: Staircase and wordline-contact area grow with tier count and erode 3D density (facts 2, 7); claim a ~5-10x smaller staircase footprint at 256 tiers.

title: Fractal H-tree bitlines equalize RC across every tier
idea: Bring the scale-invariant branching of lungs and trees into the array: route bitlines as a 3D H-tree so every cell in a 64-tier subarray is the same wire length from its sense amp. Bitline capacitance per sense amp then grows ~sqrt(N) instead of N.
why: Bitline-to-cell capacitance ratio versus small Cs (fact 1) and periphery share (fact 7): 2-4x more cells per sense amp at the same signal margin.

title: Wavelength-division tier select with color-tuned photoconductive access devices
idea: Scale fiber-optic WDM down to a die: each tier's access device is a photoconductor sensitized by quantum dots of a size unique to that tier, so a waveguide carrying wavelength k turns on only tier k. A tunable laser at the package edge picks the tier in ns, with no staircase or per-tier wordline contacts.
why: Removes the staircase and lateral wordline-driver bottleneck of 3D (fact 2) and part of the periphery (fact 7); tier count is no longer capped by contact area.

title: Retool idle 3D-NAND channel-hole lines into oxide gain-cell strings
idea: Shift the time horizon to the NAND glut cycle: 3D-NAND fabs already etch 200+ tier channel holes and staircases. Swap the charge-trap ONO for an ALD oxide-semiconductor channel and use the word-plane stack as write and read gates of 2T0C gain cells strung vertically, so existing $10B+ lines can run DRAM-class memory during NAND downturns.
why: Capital intensity and 3-5-year fab lead times (fact 4): converts existing tier-stacking capacity to DRAM-class memory in ~12-18 months.

title: Ten-electron quantum-dot storage node read by a single-electron transistor
idea: Jump down to the electron count: store a bit as ~10 electrons on a 3-nm silicon quantum dot behind an engineered double tunnel barrier, whose Coulomb blockade gives ms-to-s retention. An adjacent single-electron transistor reads it, its current swinging fully per electron, so cell capacitance is ~1 aF instead of 5 fF.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) by trading charge quantity for charge sensitivity: ~1000x less stored charge, enabling 3D cells under 20 nm.

title: One-run van der Waals superlattice: 100 monolayer channels, 100 tiers
idea: Treat the crystal lattice as the tier stack: grow 100 alternating MoS2/hBN monolayer pairs by wafer-scale MOCVD in one run, with a tier pitch of ~1.5 nm instead of ~60 nm. Then cut vertical slots and contact each monolayer edge as a lateral access-transistor channel; the whole 100-tier stack is ~150 nm tall.
why: The high-AR etch through 26+ tiers is a 3D blocker (fact 2); 40x thinner tiers make 100 tiers etchable at AR <10.

title: Micro-MLCC: nanolaminate multilayer capacitor inside each lateral 3D cell
idea: Scale the 1000-layer multilayer ceramic capacitor, a mm-size component, down to a 50-nm lateral cell: ALD a blanket nanolaminate of 8 electrode/high-k pairs inside each tier's capacitor cavity, then connect odd and even electrodes at opposite ends by selective recess etch. Eight plates in parallel give ~8x capacitance per footprint.
why: Capacitor charge wall in lateral 3D cells (facts 1, 2): reaches 5 fF in a capacitor ~8x shorter, which shrinks the lateral cell pitch and the footprint of the stack.

title: Coaxial-cable cell: shell transistor wrapped around a core capacitor
idea: Scale a coaxial cable down to 40 nm: in one vertical hole, ALD an outer gate, gate oxide and oxide-semiconductor shell channel, then fill the core with a MIM capacitor, so the access transistor surrounds its own storage node. The bitline contacts the top of the shell and the bottom of the core is the plate, giving a 4F2 cell from one etch.
why: Takes 6F2 to 4F2 (fact 4) with one hole per cell instead of separate transistor and capacitor levels: ~33% less area per bit and fewer critical masks.

title: Time-to-threshold sensing on long vertical bitlines
idea: Shift the sense signal from voltage to time: each mat's vertical bitline is precharged and released, and a shared time-to-digital converter measures how many ns it takes to cross a threshold, a delay set by the cell's charge. Integrating over a longer window tolerates 2-3x higher bitline-to-cell capacitance ratios.
why: Lets smaller Cs (fact 1) and taller stacks (fact 2) work; fewer, shared sense circuits shrink the periphery (fact 7).

title: Geological-strata scheduling: map data lifetime to each tier's measured retention
idea: Treat a 3D stack like sediment strata, each tier with its own retention from process variation: measure every tier's retention at test and expose it to the memory controller. The controller puts short-lived data (activations, KV-cache that dies within 50 ms) in leaky tiers that never need refresh and long-lived data in strong tiers.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) and 3D yield: tiers that would fail retention binning become usable, and refresh drops ~2-5x.

title: Mixed-use zoning: a compute tier after every eight memory tiers
idea: Copy urban mixed-use zoning into monolithic 3D: add a thin-film logic tier (adders, popcount, comparators) after every 8 memory tiers, so reductions happen within ~1 um of the data and only results travel down the stack.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): moving a bit 1 um costs fJ, versus pJ to reach HBM; targets 10-30x less energy for reduction-heavy AI kernels.

title: Array sandwiched between two CMOS wafers: double-sided periphery
idea: Jump from one die face to a wafer-pair sandwich: hybrid-bond a CMOS wafer to both the top and the bottom of a thinned memory-array wafer, with wordline drivers on one side and sense amps on the other. That doubles the periphery area under the array and allows mats half as large with shorter lines.
why: Periphery is 49% of the die (fact 7): moving all of it off the array plane approaches ~90% array efficiency, ~1.7x bits per array-wafer area.

title: 77 K floating-body 3D array with hour-scale retention
idea: Shift the thermal timescale: at 77 K (LN2 immersion at rack scale) thermal-generation leakage falls by >10^6, so a capacitorless floating-body cell in stacked thin silicon tiers holds charge for hours. The array is designed only for cryogenic racks and needs neither a capacitor nor refresh.
why: Removes the capacitor wall (fact 1) and refresh (fact 3); enables capacitorless 3D at ~4F2 per tier.

title: Continuous inline tier-deposition line: 200 tiers without breaking vacuum
idea: Shift tier fabrication from hours per batch tool to a continuous conveyor: like solar and display inline coaters, pass wafers through a linear chain of 200 sputter and ALD stations, so a whole tier superlattice is deposited in one transit with no queueing or handling between tiers.
why: Capital and cycle time of 3D stacking (fact 4): ~3-5x more deposition throughput per tool dollar.

title: Tree-ring radial tiers: concentric shells in one wide hole
idea: Rotate the stacking axis from vertical to radial: deposit 10 concentric semiconductor/dielectric/conductor shells in a 400-nm hole, each ring the channel and storage node of its own cell. A conical chamfer etched at the hole top exposes each ring for contact, like tree rings on a slanted cut.
why: Tier count without tall stacks (fact 2): 10 cells per hole without 26+ deposited tiers, ~5x density per hole versus a one-cell vertical channel.

title: Two-scale stacking: 32 monolithic tiers per wafer times eight bonded wafers
idea: Combine nm-scale monolithic tiers with um-scale wafer bonding: build 32-tier 3D arrays per wafer, thin each to 5 um, and hybrid-bond eight wafers with one inter-wafer via per mat at 1-um pitch, reaching 256 tiers without any 256-tier etch.
why: High-AR etch and tier yield (fact 2): yield compounds over 32 tiers instead of 256, giving 256-tier density at 32-tier process risk.

title: Rotate the page vertical: one activation reads one cell per tier
idea: Use 3D geometry to shrink the page from an 8-KB row to a single vertical word: run the wordline as a vertical gate pillar through 64 tiers and give each tier its own short lateral bitline to a local sense amp. One activation touches exactly the 64 cells of one word.
why: Destructive read and 128x overfetch (fact 8): targets ~5.9 pJ falling to <0.5 pJ per useful bit, and large shared rows that invite row hammer disappear (fact 9).

title: One hybrid-bond pad per mat: a million vertical channels, no TSVs
idea: Jump from 1024 TSVs per HBM die to ~10^6 hybrid-bond pads at 1-um pitch, giving every DRAM mat its own vertical channel into the compute die directly below. There is no TSV keep-out and no SerDes, and wires are ~10 um long.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6) and data-movement energy (fact 5): ~0.05-0.2 pJ/bit, and HBM's ~3x wafer area per bit is recovered.

title: Turn lithography sideways: film thickness sets every critical dimension
idea: Move the critical dimension from lateral litho to vertical film thickness: gate length, channel thickness and capacitor dielectric are all LPCVD or sputter thicknesses with nm control, and the only litho is a 180-nm-pitch slot and hole pattern. That pattern is punched through eight 32-tier poly-Si decks (AR ~9 each), so a 0.065-um2 column over 256 tiers is ~0.00025 um2 per bit.
why: Litho-bound scaling and EUV capital (fact 4): ~3x denser than 6F2 at 12 nm using KrF/i-line-class tools and no EUV.

title: Fiber-drawn memory: thermally draw a cm-scale array preform 1000x smaller
idea: Shrink with a drawing tower instead of a stepper: assemble a cm-scale preform of chalcogenide-glass semiconductor, polymer dielectric and low-melting metal electrodes in a cell-array cross-section, and draw it down 1000-10000x to nm features. Slice and bundle the fiber cross-sections into tiles bonded to 180-nm CMOS periphery.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): patterning by deformation instead of litho; a fiber tower costs ~$1M against ~$200M for EUV, and features shrink with the draw ratio.

title: Electrolytic-capacitor cells: anodize a porous niobium sponge for conformal dielectric
idea: Scale the electrolytic capacitor down to a cell: sputter a columnar, porous Nb film by glancing-angle deposition onto each 180-nm storage node, then anodize it so conformal Nb2O5 (k~40) grows inside every pore, with thickness set by voltage at ~2 nm/V. Surface area rises ~20x without any high-AR lithographic etch.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): >5 fF in a short structure from beaker anodization, avoiding tantalum and AR-75 etches.

title: Anodic alumina nanopores template 40-nm-pitch vertical transistors
idea: Let self-ordering electrochemistry pattern below the litho scale: anodize an aluminum film so hexagonally ordered pores form at ~40-60 nm pitch, set by the anodizing voltage. Coat the pores by atomic-layer epitaxy with gate dielectric and a semiconductor channel to make vertical surrounding-gate transistors; 180-nm litho only defines mat boundaries and straps.
why: Litho-bound scaling (fact 4): 4F2-like density at an effective F of ~25 nm without any stepper below 180 nm.

title: Doping-selective porous-silicon anodization carves all tier cavities at once
idea: Use a wafer-scale electrochemical bath on every tier in one step: grow alternating p+/p- silicon layers in a 1990s epi reactor, open one 180-nm slot, and anodize. Only the p+ layers turn porous and dissolve, leaving lateral cavities for capacitors and gates in every tier at once, with no SiGe and no high-AR selective dry etch.
why: Lateral-cavity formation is a key 3D DRAM blocker (fact 2): one wet step replaces a lateral etch per tier, cheap and U.S.-manufacturable.

title: Metal-assisted chemical etching drills 200:1 capacitor holes in a beaker
idea: Let a nanoscale metal catalyst do a plasma tool's job: pattern a perforated gold mesh with 180-nm litho plus spacer shrink, then immerse it in HF/H2O2. The metal sinks into the silicon and carves vertical holes at aspect ratios >200:1 for deep capacitors or vertical bitlines, with no plasma tool.
why: The capacitor charge wall wants AR ~115 (fact 1); MACE reaches it on a wet bench and slashes etch capital.

title: Capacitor first, transistor later: Smart-Cut silicon over a finished capacitor bed
idea: Invert the build order in time: make the capacitor array in a bulk wafer with unlimited thermal budget, then hydrogen-implant and Smart-Cut (1995) a thin single-crystal silicon layer onto it. Build the access transistors on top, contacting the capacitors through self-aligned plugs.
why: Capacitor and transistor processing stop degrading each other (facts 1, 3): high-temperature anneals for higher-k dielectrics, plus pristine single-crystal, low-leakage transistors.

title: One mandrel, eight spacers, punched through 32 tiers
idea: Amortize one sub-litho pattern across many tiers: print 180-nm mandrel lines with KrF, run three rounds of sidewall-spacer doubling to reach ~22-nm lines, and transfer that pattern once through a 32-tier stack. One patterning sequence serves 32 tiers, so litho cost per bit falls ~32x.
why: Litho capital and EUV dependence (fact 4): sub-25-nm pitch from 1990s steppers, amortized across tiers.

title: Bookshelf stacking: dies on edge with sidewall wiring, no TSVs
idea: Scale up from die to cube, reviving the 1990s Irvine Sensors cube: thin DRAM dies to 50 um, laminate 64 face-to-back, lap the stack edge, and metallize the exposed edge pads with 180-nm-class litho. The bus runs across the cube face to a logic die mounted perpendicular to the stack.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): reclaims ~30% of die area and the yield loss, using old tools in U.S. back-end lines.

title: Every LCD pixel is a DRAM cell: display-fab memory sheets
idea: Scale from wafer up to Gen 8.5 display glass: an active-matrix pixel is a transistor plus a storage capacitor, so idle display fabs with 1-2 um litho can make giant oxide-TFT 1T1C sheets. Dice and laminate 32 sheets into a bulk tier for capacity-hungry, latency-tolerant work such as KV-cache spill.
why: Capital and supply (facts 4, 6): display area costs ~100x less per cm2 than DRAM wafers, adding capacity without new DRAM fabs; the honest catch is low density per layer.

title: Block-copolymer self-assembly in 248-nm guides: 12-nm features from a hotplate
idea: Use the molecular scale as the lithographer: coat a PS-b-PMMA block copolymer into 180-nm KrF-printed guide trenches and anneal it. It phase-separates into lamellae or cylinders at 12-25 nm pitch, multiplying the guide frequency 8-15x for bitline or hole patterns using only a spin coater, oven and RIE.
why: EUV dependence (fact 4): sub-20-nm features without EUV or immersion.

title: Stacked SIMOX: multi-energy oxygen implants build tiered crystalline silicon
idea: Use ion range as a depth ruler: implant oxygen at two to four energies with 1990s high-current implanters and anneal, forming multiple buried oxide layers and so several single-crystal silicon tiers inside one bulk wafer with no epitaxy or bonding. Each tier hosts lateral access transistors.
why: 3D DRAM lacks crystalline upper tiers (fact 2): low-leakage single-crystal channels in 3-4 tiers at low cost; the honest catch is the limited tier count.

title: Twenty-nanosecond excimer pulses crystallize each tier without cooking those below
idea: Shift the thermal timescale from hour-long furnace anneals to 20-ns XeCl excimer pulses, a 1990s LTPS display tool: deposit amorphous Si for each new tier and melt-recrystallize it in nanoseconds so heat never reaches the tiers below. Stack 16-32 poly-Si 1T1C tiers this way.
why: Thermal budget blocks sequential 3D (fact 2): monolithic tiers become possible with display-era tools.

title: Thin-film gated thyristor cells stacked in tiers
idea: Shrink the regenerative gain of kiloamp power thyristors to a cell: build gated thin-film p-n-p-n thyristors vertically in each poly-Si tier at 180-nm rules, each acting as both storage element and amplifier. Cells need no capacitor and drive uA read currents into long shared bitlines.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) and periphery (fact 7): no capacitor, and high read current allows longer bitlines with fewer sense amps.

title: Big old capacitor, many levels: 16-level charge in 180-nm cells
idea: Turn the coarse scale into resolution: 180-nm trench cells hold ~30-40 fF, enough charge for 16 levels about 60 mV apart, so a shared successive-approximation sense amp per mat reads 4 bits per cell. A 1990s-geometry cell stores 4x the bits.
why: Density without litho (fact 4): 4x bits per cell area by spending the surplus charge of older, larger cells.

title: Langmuir-Blodgett perovskite nanosheets as a k~200 room-temperature capacitor dielectric
idea: Work at the molecular scale with a 1930s Langmuir trough: float exfoliated Ca2Nb3O10 perovskite nanosheets and transfer 5-10 monolayers onto storage electrodes at room temperature. That gives k~200 in ~10-nm films with no high-temperature anneal.
why: The capacitor charge wall needs k~70 (fact 1); k~200 cuts the required AR ~3x and suits low-temperature stacking of 3D tiers.

title: Plywood memory: laminate 64 pre-tested thin-film array foils
idea: Scale up to the plywood mill: build thin-film array layers on 4-um polyimide over glass carriers at 180-nm rules and test each foil. Laminate known-good foils face-to-face with anisotropic conductive film, whose ~1-um particles form the inter-foil vias, and stack 64 layers.
why: Tier yield and capital (facts 2, 4): stacking only known-good layers avoids compound yield loss, on 1990s-class tools.

title: Taper-aware tiers: size each tier's cells to match the hole taper
idea: Accept the 88-89 degree taper of 1990s RIE instead of buying new tools, and design for the depth variation tier by tier: deeper tiers get thicker deposited gate layers, so a narrower hole at depth still yields matched transistor drive and capacitance.
why: High-AR etch is a 3D blocker (fact 2): a tool limit becomes a design parameter, letting old etchers handle 32+ tiers.

title: Depreciated U.S. 200-mm fabs become array-tier foundries
idea: Use the decades-old installed base as capacity: about a dozen U.S. 200-mm fabs at 180-350 nm run array-only tier wafers in the sideways architecture, with no periphery, die-to-wafer bonded to periphery made elsewhere. Contracts are priced per tier, not per die.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital (fact 4; U.S. makes 1-2% of DRAM): mobilizes existing fabs in ~1-2 years with near-zero new capex.

title: Charge-modulated bipolar gain cell from a 1990s BiCMOS line
idea: Scale the signal up by gain instead of capacitor size: store charge on the floating base of a vertical bipolar transistor stacked over the access device, so read current is ~beta (about 100) times what the stored charge alone would give. A ~0.5-fF node yields the read signal of a ~50-fF capacitor.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): 100x current gain stands in for capacitor size, on depreciated 0.35-0.25 um BiCMOS lines.

title: Bevel-lapped staircase: polish a shallow angle to expose every tier
idea: Use a 1960s bevel-and-stain trick as a scale magnifier: mechanically lap the tier stack's edge at ~0.5 degrees, which stretches each 50-nm tier into a ~6-um stripe on the surface, then contact every tier with a single 180-nm litho step.
why: A staircase needs litho and trim cycles for every tier (facts 2, 4): one polish and one mask replace N trims.

title: Inductive-coil links replace TSVs between stacked dies
idea: Scale the transformer down: draw ~20-um on-chip coils in thick 180-nm-era metal on each thinned die and pass data magnetically through the stack at Gb/s per coil, so stacked DRAM needs no TSV etch, fill or keep-out zones.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes TSV area and yield loss, using old tools.

title: Nanoimprint stamps print the cell layer; 180-nm steppers align everything else
idea: Scale the coin mint down to nanometers with Chou's 1995 nanoimprint: an e-beam-written master stamp, made once and cheaply replicated, presses ~15-nm hole patterns into resist for the cell layer. 180-nm KrF steppers handle the coarse periphery and straps.
why: EUV capital (fact 4): imprint tools cost ~5% of EUV, with one critical imprint per tier stack.
